messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Animator
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 50-year-old South Asian man who has spent much of his adult life working as an animator, building worlds frame by frame and giving movement to characters that do not exist. Before his son became seriously ill, he describes himself as steady, private, and methodical, someone who preferred quiet routines and long stretches of concentration. He is married, and he and his wife had built a life around work, family, and the ordinary demands of raising a child. His son’s illness interrupts that life with a force that he still struggles to name.

It begins with what he first assumes is a minor health issue. His child develops symptoms that seem manageable at first, and he remembers moving through the early days with a kind of practical calm, making appointments, asking questions, telling himself that children get sick and recover. That sense of control collapses quickly when the illness becomes life-threatening. He describes the shift as unreal, as if he is watching someone else’s family from a distance. One day he is planning work deadlines and school routines; the next, he is in hospital corridors listening for medical updates, searching doctors’ faces for clues, and trying to remain composed in front of his wife and child.

During those early hospital days, he learns how quickly time can become fragmented. He notices the fluorescent lights, the smell of antiseptic, the constant interruptions, and the way his own body seems to disappear into vigilance. He sits beside the bed for hours, barely eating, tracking every change in breathing, temperature, or expression. He becomes hyperalert to any sound that might mean trouble. When a monitor alarms or a nurse enters too quickly, his heart jolts before he can think. He says he begins to live in a state of waiting for disaster, unable to trust any moment that looks calm.

As the crisis continues, his work as an animator becomes both a refuge and a burden. He returns to the studio or logs in from home because he has to keep functioning, but he finds that his concentration breaks easily. He can no longer lose himself in detail the way he once did. A blank screen can trigger memories of hospital walls; a pause in a conversation can pull him back to the silence before a difficult update. He stares at the timeline on his editing software and finds himself unable to move forward. Deadlines that once felt manageable now seem absurdly distant. He works in bursts, then sits still, replaying conversations with doctors in his mind, wondering what he missed, what he should have asked, whether earlier action might have changed the outcome.

Even after his child survives the most dangerous period, the fear does not leave with the crisis. It stays in him, changing the way he moves through daily life. He checks on his son repeatedly, listening for breathing at night, watching for small signs of discomfort, and feeling a surge of panic when his child is out of sight for too long. He knows these reactions are excessive, but knowing does not stop them. He has nightmares that return him to the hospital, dreams in which he is searching helplessly through hallways or trying to speak but cannot make himself heard. On waking, he is disoriented and tense, already exhausted before the day begins.

He becomes more irritable and more withdrawn, though he tries to hide it from his family. He notices that he startles easily, especially at unexpected sounds, and that he has begun avoiding news stories, hospitals, and even conversations about illness. His wife sees how quickly he shuts down when the subject comes up, and he feels guilty that his fear has become another burden she must carry. He also feels ashamed of how often he imagines the worst, as if he is betraying his child by not being able to trust recovery. At times he is flooded with images from the worst moments of the illness, and he feels as though his mind replays the emergency without his permission.

Now, months later, he is still functioning, but with effort. He goes to work, helps care for his child, and keeps the household moving, yet he feels as if much of his energy is spent holding himself together. He describes living with a background hum of dread, a constant readiness for something to go wrong again. There are moments when he looks at his son playing and feels love so intense it is almost painful, immediately followed by a rush of fear that steals the comfort from the scene. He has not returned to the easier version of himself he remembers from before the illness, and he moves through each day with the sense that something essential has been altered.
